newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus cabinet to be reshuffled.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus cabinet to be reshuffled.

text.p: The Cyprus cabinet resigned on Tuesday to enable a government reshuffle 10 months before the latest date that presidential elections are due on the eastern mediterranean island.
The new composition of the centre-right government will be announced later on Tuesday or early on Wednesday, government spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides told reporters.

He described the reshuffle as an act of "renewal" and did not link it to any need of the government to spruce up its image to boost President Glafcos Clerides's chances for re-election next year if he decided to run again.
"It is a political deed," he said. "Governments are reshuffled to provide a breath of fresh air, a new image," Cassoulides said.
It is the first cabinet reshuffle since Clerides, a veteran right-wing politician and founder of the Democratic Rally party, was elected president for a five-year term in February 1993.

Clerides's Greek Cypriot administration is recognised as the only legitimate government in Cyprus, which has been divided since Turkey invaded its north in 1974 in response to a brief coup engineered by the colonels ruling in Greece at the time.

Clerides himself did not elaborate on the reasons for the reshuffle either. "It is simple. I wanted a renewal of the council of ministers," he said in brief comments to reporters on the steps of the presidential palace.
Local media has tipped Cassoulides as a likely candidate for foreign minister, replacing Alecos Michaelides.

Michaelides, whose family firm owns a string of hotels on the holiday island, was recently accused by the opposition of abusing his position to secure relaxations in building permits for hotels in areas with building restrictions.
The government, which has been tight-lipped on the subject, has not given any indication this was a reason to prompt the reshuffle.
"If he (the president) has reached the decision to proceed with a reshuffle it is a political act for government renewal and not because he has any grievances with any minister," Cassoulides said.
Media reports have speculated that five of the eleven ministers, appointees of the Democratic Party which is a junior partner in the government, will be unaffected by the reshuffle.
